title: Teachers Deserve Better Access to Educational Evidence
author: Jim Hewitt and Nidhi Sachdeva
summary: Hewitt and Sachdeva argue that teachers are surrounded by confident, conflicting claims about what works in the classroom, and that the raw research literature is too vast and fragmented for most classroom teachers to sort through on their own. In response, they built a tool called The Evidence Checker: a structured prompt teachers paste into ChatGPT or another AI system, designed to push the model toward cautious, evidence-informed answers rather than slogans or simplistic best-practice lists. The authors situate the tool within a longer critique of how educational ideas normally reach teachers -- filtered through consultants, publishers, and professional-development providers who often present ideas with more certainty than the evidence supports. They argue this intermediary structure is a major driver of 'instructional churn,' the cycle of fads and oversimplified solutions that has long plagued education. Generative AI, they suggest, offers teachers a way to interrogate claims directly, ask follow-up questions, and build a more evidence-informed professional judgment rather than simply trusting what they are told. The piece is explicit that the tool is not perfect and does not replace professional judgment, but frames it as a step toward redistributing power over educational evidence away from gatekeepers and toward classroom teachers themselves.
points: The Evidence Checker is not itself an AI model but a structured prompt teachers paste into ChatGPT or a similar system, engineered to force critical evaluation of evidence strength rather than generate confident-sounding but shallow answers.

The authors trace teachers' historical dependence on intermediaries (consultants, PD providers, publishers, advocacy groups) as a structural cause of 'instructional churn' -- ideas reaching classrooms simplified, reframed, and oversold relative to what the underlying research actually supports.

Their argument reframes AI's value for teachers away from content generation and toward research literacy: the real power is in follow-up questioning that lets a teacher probe nuance, meta-analyses, and comparative strength of evidence.

The piece positions unequal access to research interpretation as a power and accountability problem in education, not just a knowledge gap -- those who lead PD have controlled the evidence narrative, while teachers were expected to trust the summary handed to them.
quotes: Teachers can end up not knowing who or what to trust. How do you figure out which ideas are actually supported by strong evidence?
The prompt is specifically designed to push the AI toward evidence-informed, nuanced, and cautious responses.

This is one of the reasons why education has historically been so susceptible to instructional churn: fads, oversimplified solutions, and highly confident ideas that spread rapidly despite limited or inconsistent supporting evidence.

In part, this has been an issue of power and accountability. Those who lead professional development have often occupied the privileged role of interpreting research, while classroom teachers were expected to trust the summaries and presentations given to them.

For the first time, many teachers may now have a practical way to directly interrogate educational claims, compare competing perspectives, ask follow-up questions, and explore what stronger forms of evidence actually suggest.

Teaching is too important to be driven by slogans, trends, and competing ideologies. Teachers deserve better access to evidence, better tools for evaluating claims, and more opportunities to think critically about what actually helps students learn.
